title: REST — Representational State Transfer
explanation:
## What is REST?

REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style introduced by Roy Fielding in his 2000 doctoral dissertation. It defines a set of constraints for building scalable web services over HTTP — not a rigid protocol, but a set of architectural principles.

## The 6 REST Constraints

**1. Stateless** — Every request must contain all information needed to process it. The server holds no client session state between calls, enabling frictionless horizontal scaling.

**2. Uniform Interface** — Resources are identified by URIs. Manipulation is performed through standard HTTP verbs. Responses are self-descriptive via Content-Type headers.

**3. Client-Server Separation** — Frontend and backend are completely decoupled. They evolve independently as long as the contract remains stable.

**4. Cacheable** — Responses must declare whether they are cacheable using `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, and `Last-Modified` headers.

**5. Layered System** — Clients do not know (or care) whether they connect directly to the origin server, a CDN cache, or an API gateway.

**6. Code on Demand (optional)** — Servers can optionally return executable code (like JavaScript) to clients.

## HTTP Verbs & Semantics

```
GET    /users        → List all users           (safe, idempotent)
GET    /users/42     → Fetch user #42           (safe, idempotent)
POST   /users        → Create a new user        (not idempotent)
PUT    /users/42     → Replace user #42 fully   (idempotent)
PATCH  /users/42     → Update specific fields   (idempotent)
DELETE /users/42     → Remove user #42          (idempotent)
```

## Standard Status Codes

```
200 OK           — Successful GET / PATCH
201 Created      — POST that created a resource (with Location header)
204 No Content   — DELETE or PUT with no body returned
400 Bad Request  — Malformed request syntax / validation failure
401 Unauthorized — Missing or invalid authentication token
403 Forbidden    — Authenticated but lacks required permission
404 Not Found    — Target resource does not exist
429 Too Many Requests — Rate limit threshold exceeded
500 Internal Error — Unexpected server-side failure
```

## Real-World Example

```http
POST /api/v1/articles HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json

{
  "title": "Understanding REST APIs",
  "content": "REST is an architectural style...",
  "tags": ["api", "web"]
}

# Response:
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /api/v1/articles/108
Content-Type: application/json
ETag: W/"33a64df551425fcc55e4d42a148795d9f25f89d4"

{
  "id": 108,
  "title": "Understanding REST APIs",
  "status": "published",
  "createdAt": "2026-09-11T00:00:00Z"
}
```

## Industry Best Practices

**Nouns not verbs in URIs** — Use `/orders` instead of `/createOrder` or `/getOrders`.

**Plural resource names** — Standardize on `/users` and `/users/{id}` for consistency.

**API versioning** — Use URI path prefix `/v1/users` or Header-based versioning `Accept: application/vnd.company.v1+json`.

**Pagination & Filtering** — Return structured metadata for collections: `?page=2&limit=20&sort=-createdAt`.

comparisonPoints.value: GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; POST is not

title: SOAP — Simple Object Access Protocol
explanation:
## What is SOAP?

SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) is a W3C-standard messaging protocol designed for exchanging structured, strongly-typed information in enterprise distributed environments. Unlike REST's architectural flexibility, SOAP is a **strict specification** built on XML.

## Anatomy of a SOAP Message

Every SOAP message is an XML document packaged into an **Envelope** with four distinct sections:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<soap:Envelope xmlns:soap="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/"
               xmlns:web="http://api.example.com/banking">
  <soap:Header>
    <!-- Optional: Security tokens, routing metadata, transaction IDs -->
    <wsse:Security xmlns:wsse="http://docs.oasis-open.org/wss/2004/01/...">
      <wsse:UsernameToken>
        <wsse:Username>agent_47</wsse:Username>
        <wsse:Password>SecretDigest123</wsse:Password>
      </wsse:UsernameToken>
    </wsse:Security>
  </soap:Header>
  <soap:Body>
    <!-- Mandatory: The actual payload / RPC invocation -->
    <web:TransferFunds>
      <web:FromAccount>ACC-9921</web:FromAccount>
      <web:ToAccount>ACC-1044</web:ToAccount>
      <web:Amount currency="USD">5000.00</web:Amount>
    </web:TransferFunds>
  </soap:Body>
</soap:Envelope>
```

## WSDL — The Strict Service Contract

WSDL (Web Services Description Language) is an XML schema describing the entire API contract:
- Available operations and methods
- Input/Output data types and constraints (XSD validation)
- Network endpoint address and binding protocols

Because WSDL is strictly typed, enterprise client code (Java stubs, C# classes) can be auto-generated with zero manual typing.

## WS-Security & Enterprise Standards

SOAP features built-in enterprise extensions maintained by OASIS:
- **WS-Security**: End-to-end XML message signing & encryption (tamper-proof even across multiple intermediary proxies)
- **WS-ReliableMessaging**: Guarantees exactly-once message delivery over lossy networks
- **WS-AtomicTransaction**: Distributed ACID transactions across multi-system boundaries

## When to Use SOAP

- **Financial Services & Banking** (SWIFT, core banking ledgers)
- **Healthcare Systems** (HL7 EHR data integrations)
- **Legacy Enterprise Backbones** (SAP, Oracle, IBM WebSphere)

title: GraphQL — Query Language for APIs
API Authentication & Authorization
explanation:
## Authentication vs Authorization

- **Authentication (AuthN)**: *Who are you?* (Verifying identity via API Key, Password, Token)
- **Authorization (AuthZ)**: *What are you allowed to do?* (Permissions, Scopes, Role-Based Access Control)

## Common API Authentication Methods

### 1. API Keys
Simple static tokens passed in headers. Best for machine-to-machine integrations or developer SDKs.
```http
GET /v1/weather HTTP/1.1
X-API-Key: sk_live_9a8b7c6d5e4f3a2b1c
```

### 2. Bearer Tokens & JWT (JSON Web Tokens)
Stateless, cryptographically signed tokens containing user payload and expiry claims.

```
JWT Structure: [Header].[Payload].[Signature]

Header:    {"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"}
Payload:   {"sub": "usr_102", "role": "player", "exp": 1773000000}
Signature: HMACSHA256(base64(Header) + "." + base64(Payload), secret)
```

Sent in the standard Authorization header:
```http
GET /v1/profile HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsIn...
```

### 3. OAuth 2.0 & OpenID Connect (OIDC)
Delegated authorization framework for third-party access (e.g., "Sign in with Google/GitHub").

- **Authorization Code Flow + PKCE**: The modern gold standard for SPAs and mobile apps
- **Client Credentials Flow**: Server-to-server automated background services

## Security Best Practices

- Always enforce HTTPS/TLS to protect tokens in transit
- Keep Access Token lifetimes short (e.g. 15 minutes) and rotate Refresh Tokens
- Never store access tokens in `localStorage` if vulnerable to XSS; use `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookies
- Validate token signatures, issuer (`iss`), audience (`aud`), and expiration (`exp`) on every request

comparisonPoints.value: Short-lived access tokens (15m) + refresh token rotation

title: API Pagination Strategies
explanation:
## Why Pagination is Essential

Loading thousands of database records in a single API response leads to high memory consumption, sluggish database queries, network latency, and client crashes. Pagination splits large datasets into predictable, bite-sized pages.

## The Three Major Pagination Strategies

### 1. Offset-Based Pagination
Using `page` and `limit` (or `offset` and `limit`):
```http
GET /v1/items?offset=40&limit=20 HTTP/1.1
```
- **SQL Equivalent**: `SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40`
- **Pros**: Easy to implement, supports direct "jump to page N"
- **Cons**: Slow on deep pages (`OFFSET 1000000` scans 1M rows); causes duplicates/skips if records are added/deleted while paging

### 2. Keyset / Cursor-Based Pagination
Using an opaque pointer to the last seen record:
```http
GET /v1/items?limit=20&after=eyJpZCI6MTA0Mn0= HTTP/1.1
```
- **SQL Equivalent**: `SELECT * FROM items WHERE id > 1042 ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT 20`
- **Pros**: Blazing fast (`O(1)` indexed seek regardless of depth), immune to phantom rows and data shifts
- **Cons**: Cannot jump to arbitrary page numbers (sequential forward/back only)

### 3. Time-Window Pagination
Using timestamps (`since` and `until`) for append-only time-series feeds (logs, analytics, chat history).

## Standard Response Headers (RFC 5988)

Use the `Link` header for navigation links:
```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Link: <https://api.example.com/v1/items?page=3&limit=20>; rel="next",
      <https://api.example.com/v1/items?page=1&limit=20>; rel="prev",
      <https://api.example.com/v1/items?page=50&limit=20>; rel="last"
```

comparisonPoints.label: Offset Paging
comparisonPoints.value: Simple ?page=1&limit=20, supports jumping to arbitrary page

comparisonPoints.label: Cursor Paging
comparisonPoints.value: O(1) index seek, immune to record insertions/deletions

comparisonPoints.label: Performance
comparisonPoints.value: Cursor pagination scales to billions of records seamlessly

comparisonPoints.label: Best For
comparisonPoints.value: Social feeds, infinite scroll, real-time activity logs

title: Rate Limiting & Throttling
explanation:
## Why APIs Need Rate Limiting

Rate limiting controls the frequency of incoming requests to protect infrastructure from DDoS attacks, prevent brute-force credential stuffing, ensure fair tenant resource distribution, and enforce monetization tier quotas.

## Core Rate Limiting Algorithms

### 1. Token Bucket
A bucket fills with tokens at a constant rate `r` up to capacity `b`. Each request consumes 1 token. If the bucket is empty, requests are rejected. Allows short bursts up to capacity `b` while strictly capping long-term consumption.

### 2. Leaky Bucket
Requests enter a queue (bucket) and are processed at a steady outflow rate. Excess requests overflow and are dropped immediately. Eliminates bursts and smooths out traffic spikes.

### 3. Sliding Window Counter
Combines the current window counter with the weighted percentage of the previous window to prevent boundary burst attacks where double quotas are consumed across window transitions.

## Standard Rate Limit Headers (IETF)

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
RateLimit-Limit: 100
RateLimit-Remaining: 87
RateLimit-Reset: 1773000060

# When limit exceeded:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/rate-limit-exceeded",
  "title": "Too Many Requests",
  "status": 429,
  "detail": "Quota exceeded. Please retry after 30 seconds."
}
```

## Distributed Rate Limiting with Redis

In modern microservices with multi-instance servers, rate limits are tracked in Redis using atomic Lua scripts or Redis cell modules to avoid race conditions across cluster nodes.

title: API Security & Threat Protection
explanation:
## OWASP API Security Top 10

The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) highlights the most dangerous API vulnerabilities:

### 1. Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA / IDOR)
#1 risk in APIs. Occurs when endpoints expose IDs without verifying ownership:
```http
# Attack: User 42 reads User 99's private billing
GET /api/v1/users/99/invoices
Authorization: Bearer <user_42_token>
```
- **Remediation**: Always enforce authorization checks in the data layer: `WHERE invoice.user_id = req.user.id`.

### 2. Broken Authentication
Weak passwords, unvalidated JWT signatures, missing token expirations, credentials in URLs.

### 3. Broken Object Property Level Authorization (BOPLA)
Returning sensitive fields in responses (`passwordHash`, `ssn`, `internalNotes`) or allowing mass assignment on update endpoints.

### 4. Unrestricted Resource Consumption
Missing rate limits, unbounded array payload sizes, unconstrained SQL queries.

### 5. Security Misconfiguration
Wildcard CORS headers (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with credentials), verbose stack traces exposed in production.

## Essential Security Headers Checklist

```http
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Frame-Options: DENY
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
```

## Injection Prevention
Always validate request bodies with strict schemas (e.g. Zod, Joi) and use parameterized SQL queries or ORMs (Prisma, TypeORM) to eliminate SQL injection.

comparisonPoints.value: Allowlist specific origins, never wildcard * with credentials

comparisonPoints.label: Injection

title: Error Handling & Status Codes
explanation:
## Why Structured Error Handling Matters

A good API error response tells the caller **what happened**, **why it happened**, and **how to fix it**, without exposing sensitive internal stack traces.

## HTTP Status Code Taxonomy

```
2xx Success       → Operation completed as expected
3xx Redirection   → Resource moved or cached (304 Not Modified)
4xx Client Error  → Client sent bad data, lacks auth, or requested missing resource
5xx Server Error  → Server crashed, timeout, or upstream dependency failed
```

## Essential Status Codes for APIs

- `400 Bad Request`: Malformed JSON or syntax failure
- `401 Unauthorized`: Missing or invalid authentication token
- `403 Forbidden`: Authenticated, but lacking permission to perform action
- `404 Not Found`: Target resource or endpoint does not exist
- `409 Conflict`: Resource state conflict (e.g. email already registered)
- `422 Unprocessable Entity`: Valid JSON syntax, but failed business rule validations
- `429 Too Many Requests`: Rate limit reached
- `500 Internal Server Error`: Unhandled server exception
- `502 / 503 / 504`: Gateway and upstream service failures

## RFC 7807 Problem Details (The Standard)

RFC 7807 defines the standard error envelope `application/problem+json`:

```json
{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/validation-failed",
  "title": "Validation Failed",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "One or more fields in your request failed validation.",
  "instance": "/v1/users/register",
  "invalidParams": [
    { "name": "email", "reason": "Must be a valid email format" },
    { "name": "password", "reason": "Must contain at least 8 characters" }
  ],
  "traceId": "req_902bf81a"
}
```

comparisonPoints.label: Request IDs
comparisonPoints.value: Include traceId for correlated server-side log search

comparisonPoints.label: HTTP Semantics
comparisonPoints.value: Never return HTTP 200 with an error object inside
